title: None like Moses
hookLine: his epitaph says: from Moses to Moses there arose none like Moses

lines: THE TORAH'S LAST WORDS ON MOSES.
cards: Near its very end, the Torah stops to look back at Moses. After his death, it says, no prophet has arisen in Israel like him, whom the Lord knew face to face.
Much later, Jews took that sentence and bent it, gently, to praise a second Moses. Tradition says the words came to be linked with his grave: from Moses to Moses, there arose none like Moses.
Today begins a block about the man that saying praises.

teach.b: Moses ben Maimon. In Hebrew he's usually called by an acronym, Rambam: Rabbi Moshe ben Maimon. In English, Maimonides.
The saying plays on two men named Moses: from Moses the prophet to Moses ben Maimon, none arose like this Moses. It's praise, and it's a large claim. Notice what it doesn't say.
It doesn't make him a prophet, and it doesn't put him above the first Moses. The verse in Deuteronomy reads, in the King James Bible, "there arose not a prophet since in Israel like unto Moses."

teach.h: BORROWING THE SHAPE OF A VERSE.
teach.b: The saying borrows the shape of that verse to honor a teacher. What did he teach? This block will walk through it.

teach.h: A COMMENTARY, A CODE, A GUIDE.
teach.b: He wrote a commentary on the whole Mishnah. He wrote the Mishneh Torah, the code we met in the block just closed, setting out Jewish law in clear Hebrew, in one voice.
He drew up principles of faith. He wrote the Guide for the Perplexed, for readers caught between Torah and philosophy. He worked as a physician, and wrote letters to communities in trouble.

And not everyone welcomed him. His books stirred sharp arguments, in his own time and after; some communities embraced them and some opposed them, and that's part of his story too. So why say none like Moses?
The saying ties him back to the first Moses, whom Jews call Moshe Rabbenu, Moses our teacher. It remembers Maimonides in that same line: not a lawgiver from the mountain, but a Moses who taught.

how: Maimonides' works, especially the Mishneh Torah and the Guide for the Perplexed, are studied in yeshivas, universities and synagogue classes, and the saying 'from Moses to Moses there arose none like Moses' is often quoted in his honor.

games.q: the Torah says no prophet arose in Israel like Moses. Jews later want to honor a great teacher also named Moses. what do they say?
o: he was greater than the first Moses.
from Moses to Moses there arose none like Moses.
nothing; the verse forbids any praise.
games.why: the saying links the two and honors the second as a teacher, without making him a prophet or placing him above the first.

practice: Bring to mind one teacher who shaped you, in a classroom, at a kitchen table or through a book, and let their voice come back. What did they give you that you still use?
If you pray, you can give thanks for them in your own way; if not, simply hold them in mind with gratitude.
